description: A Maharashtrian multi-flour savoury pancake made from a blend of jowar, bajra and besan — an entirely different cooking technique from any chilla, dosa or paratha, mixed and patted directly on the tawa.
instructions: Mix the three flours with onion, cumin seeds and ajwain, and enough water to form a soft, pliable dough.
Pat the dough directly onto a hot, lightly oiled tawa with wet hands into a thin round (a distinct technique from rolling with a pin).
Poke a few holes in the centre with a finger, drizzle a little oil, and cook covered until golden on both sides.
Serve hot with curd.
why_it_works: Multi-flour blend gives a broader nutrient profile than any single-grain flatbread in the database
Hand-patted-on-the-tawa technique is genuinely different from rolling a dough with a pin
Traditional Maharashtrian breakfast staple

name: ZITLAS Sabudana Thalipeeth
description: A thalipeeth made primarily from crushed sabudana and boiled potato — a fasting-day-style flour-free version, distinct from the mixed-grain thalipeeth.
instructions: Mix soaked sabudana with mashed potato, crushed peanuts, green chilli and cumin seeds into a soft dough.
Pat directly onto a hot, lightly oiled tawa into a thin round.
Cook covered until golden on both sides, flipping once.
Serve hot with curd.
Note: sabudana needs overnight soaking, not counted in active prep time above.
why_it_works: Flour-free, fasting-day-appropriate ingredient base distinct from the grain-flour thalipeeth
Same hand-patting technique applied to a genuinely different base
Peanuts supply most of the protein here

name: ZITLAS Misal Pav Bowl
description: Sprouted moth bean curry topped with crunchy farsan and served with pav — a spicier, farsan-topped format distinct from the plain Matki Usal Bowl.
ingredients: Misal masala or goda masala — 5 g
instructions: Heat oil, saute onion until golden, add tomato and cook soft.
Add boiled matki and misal masala with water to form a thin, spicy gravy; simmer 10 minutes.
Ladle into a bowl and top with a handful of farsan (store-bought or homemade thin sev) just before serving.
Serve with pav on the side.
why_it_works: The farsan topping and pav pairing make this a genuinely different eating experience from the plain Matki Usal Bowl already in the database
Iconic Maharashtrian breakfast, distinctly spicier and more textured
Filling, complete meal-style breakfast

name: ZITLAS Dabeli
description: A Kutchi-style spiced mashed potato filling stuffed into a pav with peanuts, pomegranate and chutney — a distinctly sweet-tangy-spicy regional street food not resembling any other roll or sandwich in the database.
instructions: Mash boiled potato with dabeli masala and a spoon of tamarind chutney until well combined.
Warm the mixture in a pan with a little oil.
Slice the pav and lightly toast the cut sides.
Stuff with the spiced potato, then top with roasted peanuts and pomegranate seeds before closing.
Serve warm.
why_it_works: The sweet-tart-crunchy combination of tamarind chutney, peanuts and pomegranate makes this genuinely distinct from every other bun or roll in the database
Kutchi (Gujarat) street food rarely represented in fitness recipe collections
Peanuts and pomegranate turn a simple potato filling into something texturally complex

name: ZITLAS Baked Moong Dal Kachori
description: A whole wheat kachori filled with spiced moong dal, baked instead of deep-fried — a distinct pastry-like format not represented anywhere else in the database.
ingredients: Moong dal, soaked and coarsely ground — 70 g
instructions: Cook the ground moong dal with fennel seeds, ginger and asafoetida in a dry pan until thick and moisture-free; cool.
Knead atta with a little oil and water into a firm dough.
Roll small discs, stuff with the dal filling, seal and flatten gently.
Preheat oven to 200°C and bake the kachoris for 18-20 minutes, turning once, until golden and crisp.
Serve with mint chutney.
why_it_works: Baking instead of deep-frying keeps this meaningfully lighter than a traditional kachori while keeping the flaky, stuffed pastry format
A pastry-style stuffed bread not represented anywhere else in the database
Good make-ahead batch option

name: ZITLAS Baked Vegetable Samosa Bites
description: Small whole wheat samosas filled with spiced mixed vegetables, baked rather than fried — a bite-sized version distinct from the full-size kachori.
instructions: Cook finely chopped vegetables with cumin seeds and garam masala in a dry pan until soft and moisture-free.
Knead atta with a little oil and water into a firm dough.
Roll small discs, fold into cones, stuff with the vegetable filling and seal into small triangles.
Preheat oven to 200°C and bake for 18-20 minutes, turning once, until golden and crisp.
Serve with tamarind chutney.
why_it_works: Bite-sized, baked format cuts the oil dramatically compared to deep-fried samosas while keeping the familiar shape and crunch
Vegetable-only filling distinct from the dal-filled kachori in this batch
Good for sharing or a family breakfast

name: ZITLAS Aloo Kulcha
description: A soft, curd-leavened kulcha stuffed with spiced potato — a different filling from the paneer kulcha already in the database, using the same distinct dough technique.
instructions: Knead maida with curd and water into a soft dough; rest 15 minutes.
Mash potato with onion, coriander and garam masala for the filling.
Roll out the dough, stuff with the potato filling and seal.
Roast on a hot tawa with a little oil until golden with brown spots on both sides.
Serve hot with pickle.
why_it_works: Same curd-leavened kulcha dough as the paneer version but with a distinctly different, more traditional filling
Soft, pillowy texture unlike a plain roti
Restaurant-style comfort food at home

name: ZITLAS Khaman
description: A fluffy, spongy steamed besan snack made with a different batter ratio and technique from dhokla, giving it a distinctly lighter, more porous texture.
instructions: Whisk besan with curd and water into a thin, well-beaten batter (beat vigorously for extra air, unlike a standard dhokla batter).
Add eno fruit salt and mix gently just before steaming.
Pour into a greased tin and steam for 12-15 minutes until well risen and spongy.
Cut into cubes, then temper mustard seeds and green chilli in oil and pour over the top.
why_it_works: Deliberately thinner batter and vigorous beating give khaman a distinctly spongier, lighter texture than the denser dhokla already in the database
Steamed, essentially fat-free base
Classic Gujarati street food

name: ZITLAS Rava Dhokla
description: A steamed dhokla made from semolina (rava) instead of besan — a different grain base with a distinctly grainier texture from the besan, oats, moong or multigrain versions.
instructions: Whisk rava with curd and water into a thick batter; rest 15 minutes to let the rava soften.
Add eno fruit salt just before steaming and mix gently.
Pour into a greased tin and steam for 12-15 minutes.
Cool slightly, cut into squares, and temper mustard seeds and curry leaves in oil poured over the top.
why_it_works: Semolina base gives a distinctly grainier bite from the smoother besan or moong dhokla already in the database
Faster to prepare since rava needs no grinding
Steamed, low added fat

name: ZITLAS Instant Rava Dosa
description: A thin, lacy, crisp dosa made from a rava-rice flour batter that needs no fermentation — a distinctly different texture and technique from the fermented urad-rice dosas already in the database.
instructions: Whisk rava and rice flour with plenty of water into a thin, watery batter (much thinner than a regular dosa batter); rest 15 minutes.
Mix in onion, cumin seeds and green chilli.
Pour the batter from height around the edges of a hot tawa first, then fill the centre, to create lacy holes.
Drizzle oil around the edges and cook until crisp and golden; no flipping needed.
Serve hot with chutney.
why_it_works: No-fermentation, instant technique is genuinely different from every fermented dosa or idli batter in the database
Distinctly lacy, crisp texture unlike a soft, thick dosa
Good for when there's no time to plan a fermented batter ahead

name: ZITLAS Neer Dosa
description: An ultra-thin, soft rice dosa from Mangalore made without fermentation or urad dal — a distinctly different rice-only batter and delicate texture from any other dosa in the database.
instructions: Soak rice for at least 2 hours, then grind with water into a very thin, watery batter, thinner than any other dosa batter used elsewhere.
Heat a tawa, pour a thin layer of batter and swirl quickly to spread it thin.
Cover and cook briefly until the edges lift, without flipping.
Fold gently into a soft, delicate dosa.
Serve with coconut chutney or a light curry.
Note: rice needs 2+ hours soaking, folded into prep time above.
why_it_works: Rice-only, no-urad, no-fermentation batter is genuinely distinct from every other dosa technique in the database
Delicate, soft texture (not crisp) sets it apart from Instant Rava Dosa or a regular dosa
Coastal Karnataka home cooking rarely represented in fitness recipe collections

name: ZITLAS Appam with Coconut Milk
description: A Kerala fermented rice-and-coconut-milk pancake, cooked in a curved pan for soft, spongy centres and lacy, crisp edges — a bowl-shaped format entirely unlike a flat dosa or uttapam.
instructions: Soak rice for several hours, grind with a little of the coconut milk into a smooth batter, mix in yeast and a pinch of sugar, and let ferment overnight.
Just before cooking, thin the batter with the remaining coconut milk and water.
Heat a curved appam pan (or a small kadai), pour a ladle of batter and swirl quickly up the sides.
Cover and cook until the centre is soft and set and the edges are golden and lacy.
Serve as is or with a light vegetable stew.
Note: batter needs overnight fermentation, not counted in active prep time above.
why_it_works: The curved-pan technique produces a bowl shape with a distinct soft-centre, crisp-edge texture unlike any flat dosa or uttapam in the database
Coconut milk gives a naturally mild sweetness without added sugar
Classic Kerala breakfast staple, genuinely different from Tamil or Karnataka rice preparations already represented

name: ZITLAS Puttu
description: Steamed layers of rice flour and grated coconut, cooked in a cylindrical mould — a distinctly different steamed texture (crumbly, not smooth like idli) from anything else in the database.
instructions: Sprinkle water gradually over rice flour, rubbing it in with your fingers until it reaches a coarse, breadcrumb-like consistency (not a smooth batter).
Layer the moistened flour and grated coconut alternately into a puttu mould (or a tall steamer vessel with holes).
Steam for 10-12 minutes until firm.
Unmould onto a plate and serve with banana or a light curry on the side.
why_it_works: Layered, crumbly steamed texture is entirely unlike the smooth batter of an idli or the flat shape of a dosa
No fermentation and no blending required, just a coarse hand-mixed flour
Kerala breakfast staple rarely represented in fitness recipe collections

name: ZITLAS Adai
description: A thick, savoury dosa made from a coarse blend of rice and several dals together, needing no fermentation — a distinctly different batter composition and texture from any single-dal dosa in the database.
instructions: Soak rice and all three dals together for at least 4 hours, then grind coarsely (not smooth) with red chilli and ginger.
No fermentation needed — the batter can be used right after grinding.
Heat a tawa, pour a thick ladle of batter and spread into a coarse, thick round.
Drizzle oil around the edges and cook until crisp on both sides.
Serve hot with jaggery and butter, or coconut chutney.
Note: soaking time folded into prep above.
why_it_works: Combining three dals with rice gives adai notably more protein and a coarser, heartier texture than any fermented dosa in the database
No fermentation wait needed, unlike a regular dosa
Traditional South Indian dish specifically designed around multi-pulse nutrition

name: ZITLAS Chettinad Egg Curry Bowl
description: Boiled eggs simmered in a fiery, freshly ground Chettinad-style spice paste — a distinctly different South Indian regional flavour profile from the Bengali or standard multigrain-roti egg curries in the database.
ingredients: Chettinad masala (fennel, star anise, dried chilli) — 6 g
instructions: Grind grated coconut with the Chettinad spice mix into a thick paste.
Heat oil, saute onion until golden, add tomato and cook soft.
Add the ground spice paste and a little water; simmer 8-10 minutes into a thick gravy.
Halve the boiled eggs and simmer in the gravy for 3-4 minutes.
Serve hot with rice or a plain dosa.
why_it_works: Chettinad spicing (fennel, star anise, coconut) is a genuinely distinct regional flavour direction from the Bengali panch-phoron or North Indian garam-masala egg curries already in the database
Freshly ground spice paste, not a pre-mixed masala powder
Tamil Nadu regional cuisine represented for the first time with eggs

name: ZITLAS Prawn Curry Rice Bowl
description: A light coconut-based prawn curry served over rice — introducing prawn, a seafood protein not used anywhere else in the database.
instructions: Heat oil, saute onion until soft, add turmeric and red chilli powder.
Add coconut milk and a little water, bring to a gentle simmer.
Add the prawns and cook for 4-5 minutes only, until just pink and cooked through (overcooking makes them rubbery).
Serve the curry over warm rice.
why_it_works: Prawns are a genuinely new protein source for the database, giving non-vegetarian users seafood variety beyond fish, chicken and mutton
Coconut-based gravy is light and quick to prepare
Prawns cook very fast, making this a realistically quick non-vegetarian breakfast

name: ZITLAS Lean Mutton Keema Paratha
description: A stuffed paratha filled with spiced lean mutton mince — introducing mutton, a red meat protein not used anywhere else in the database, alongside the existing chicken keema paratha.
instructions: Cook the mutton mince with onion, ginger-garlic paste and garam masala in a pan until fully cooked and fairly dry; cool slightly.
Knead atta into a dough, stuff with the cooked mince filling and seal well.
Roll out carefully and roast on a tawa with a little oil until golden and cooked through on both sides.
Serve hot with curd.
why_it_works: Mutton is a genuinely new red-meat protein source for the database, offering variety beyond chicken for non-vegetarian users
Lean mince selection keeps saturated fat more moderate than a fattier cut
Same proven stuffed-paratha technique as the chicken version, giving users a choice

name: ZITLAS Baked Kanda Bhaji Bites
description: Onion fritter batter shaped into small bites and baked instead of deep-fried — a lighter version of a popular tea-time snack, reframed for breakfast.
instructions: Mix thinly sliced onion with besan, rice flour, red chilli powder and turmeric, adding just enough water to bind (the onion releases its own moisture too).
Shape into small, loose bite-sized mounds on a lightly greased tray.
Bake at 200°C for 15-18 minutes, turning once, until golden and crisp at the edges.
Serve with chutney.
why_it_works: Baking instead of deep-frying keeps the fat dramatically lower than a traditional kanda bhaji while keeping the crisp edges
Turns a popular monsoon tea-time snack into a genuinely lighter breakfast bite
Simple, mostly hands-off baking

name: ZITLAS Methi Thepla
description: A Gujarati flatbread made with fresh fenugreek leaves worked directly into the dough — a distinct bread-making tradition (thepla) from the paneer-stuffed Methi Paneer Paratha already in the database.
instructions: Knead atta and besan with chopped methi leaves, turmeric, ajwain and a little oil and water into a firm dough.
Roll out thin (theplas are rolled thinner than a regular roti) and roast on a hot tawa with a little oil until golden with brown spots.
Serve hot, often with curd or pickle.
why_it_works: Methi is kneaded directly into the dough itself, unlike the paneer version which uses methi only as a stuffing — a genuinely different construction technique
Theplas are traditionally rolled thinner and travel well, unlike a thicker paratha
Classic Gujarati travel-food staple

name: ZITLAS Moong Dal Khichu
description: A steamed, spoonable rice-flour dumpling mixture flavoured with moong dal — a Gujarati steamed-batter format entirely unlike a chilla, dhokla or idli.
ingredients: Moong dal, cooked and mashed — 40 g
instructions: Bring water to a boil with cumin seeds and ajwain.
Slowly whisk in rice flour and mashed moong dal, stirring continuously to avoid lumps, until it thickens into a soft, cohesive dough-like mass directly in the pan.
Cover and cook on very low heat for 8-10 minutes, stirring occasionally.
Spoon into a bowl, drizzle with a little warm oil, and eat with a spoon.
why_it_works: Cooked and eaten with a spoon straight from the pan, unlike any steamed or pan-cooked dish elsewhere in the database
Moong dal addition raises protein above a plain rice-flour khichu
Simple, single-pot Gujarati home food

name: ZITLAS Egg Appam Bowl
description: Soft, spongy appam torn into pieces and served with a light egg curry — a distinct pairing from the classic coconut-stew accompaniment.
instructions: Ferment the rice-coconut milk batter overnight as for a regular appam.
Cook appams in a curved pan as usual.
Separately, saute onion in oil, add a little water and simmer the halved boiled eggs in a light gravy for 3-4 minutes.
Serve the appams with the egg curry spooned over or alongside.
Note: batter needs overnight fermentation, not counted in active prep time above.
why_it_works: Egg curry pairing raises the protein of a meal that's traditionally quite light on protein
Distinct from the standard vegetable stew accompaniment to appam
Genuinely different from any other egg preparation by the appam's soft, spongy texture

name: ZITLAS Baked Mathri Bites
description: Small, flaky whole wheat crackers, baked instead of deep-fried — a crunchy, shelf-stable snack reframed as a grab-and-go breakfast.
instructions: Knead atta with oil, ajwain, cumin seeds and just enough water into a firm, slightly stiff dough.
Roll out thick and cut into small discs, pricking each with a fork.
Bake at 180°C for 12-15 minutes until firm and lightly golden.
Cool completely — mathri crisps up further as it cools.
Store in an airtight container for up to two weeks.
why_it_works: Baking removes almost all the oil a deep-fried mathri would need while keeping the flaky crunch
Long shelf life makes this a genuine grab-and-go option for busy mornings, unlike most other recipes here
Simple ingredient list, easy to batch

name: ZITLAS Puffed Rice Upma
description: A dry, tempered upma made from puffed rice (murmura) instead of rava or poha — a different, lighter-textured upma from anything else labelled 'upma' in the database.
ingredients: Mustard seeds, curry leaves, turmeric — 3 g
instructions: Heat oil, temper mustard seeds and curry leaves, roast peanuts, then saute onion until soft.
Add turmeric and the puffed rice, tossing on low heat for just 2-3 minutes (puffed rice needs far less cooking than rava or poha).
Serve immediately while still light and crisp.
why_it_works: Puffed rice cooks in a fraction of the time of rava or poha upma and stays airier rather than dense
Genuinely different texture (light, crunchy) from the rava or poha versions already in the database
Very quick, very low cost

name: ZITLAS Baked Paneer Kachori Bites
description: Small whole wheat kachoris filled with spiced paneer, baked rather than fried — a distinct filling from the moong dal kachori already in this batch.
instructions: Mix crumbled paneer with onion, coriander and garam masala for the filling.
Knead atta with a little oil and water into a firm dough.
Roll small discs, stuff with the paneer filling, seal and flatten gently.
Bake at 200°C for 18-20 minutes, turning once, until golden.
Serve with mint chutney.
why_it_works: Paneer filling gives a softer, creamier bite than the drier moong dal kachori filling
Baked rather than fried, keeping this meaningfully lighter than a traditional kachori
Good make-ahead batch option

name: ZITLAS Sprouted Ragi Dosa
description: A dosa batter made by grinding sprouted ragi rather than plain ragi flour — a distinct preparation that changes both nutrition and flavour from the plain Ragi Dosa already in the database.
instructions: Sprout ragi grains over 1-2 days ahead of time (rinse and drain twice daily until small shoots appear), then grind with rice flour and curd into a batter.
Rest 15 minutes.
Heat a tawa, pour the batter and spread into a dosa.
Drizzle a little oil around the edges and cook until crisp, then flip briefly.
Serve hot with chutney.
Note: sprouting ragi takes 1-2 days ahead of cooking, not counted in prep time above.
why_it_works: Sprouting ragi before grinding meaningfully changes its nutrient availability and gives a noticeably different, slightly sweeter flavour from the plain-flour Ragi Dosa in the database
A genuinely different preparation process, not just a renamed dish
High fiber, naturally gluten-free

name: ZITLAS Bajra Thalipeeth
description: A single-grain bajra thalipeeth — a simpler, more traditional version distinct from the multi-flour blend used in the standard Thalipeeth recipe.
instructions: Mix bajra flour with onion, cumin seeds, green chilli and enough water to form a soft dough.
Pat directly onto a hot, lightly oiled tawa into a thin round.
Poke a few holes, drizzle oil, and cook covered until golden on both sides.
Serve hot with curd.
why_it_works: Single-grain version offers a purer bajra flavour and texture, distinct from the blended multi-flour thalipeeth
Same hand-patting technique, simpler ingredient list
Good winter-season breakfast, bajra being traditionally warming

name: ZITLAS Vegetable Adai
description: Adai batter with finely chopped vegetables mixed in before cooking — a vegetable-forward variant of the plain multi-dal Adai earlier in this batch.
instructions: Soak rice and dals together for at least 4 hours, then grind coarsely with red chilli and ginger.
Mix in finely chopped vegetables.
Heat a tawa, pour a thick ladle of batter and spread into a coarse round.
Drizzle oil around the edges and cook until crisp on both sides.
Serve hot with chutney.
why_it_works: Vegetables mixed directly into the batter make this genuinely different from the plain multi-dal adai, adding fiber and micronutrients
Same protein-dense multi-dal base, broader nutrient profile
No fermentation needed

name: ZITLAS Chicken Keema Kulcha
description: A curd-leavened kulcha stuffed with spiced chicken mince — a non-vegetarian kulcha filling distinct from the paneer or potato versions already in the database.
instructions: Cook the chicken mince with ginger-garlic paste and garam masala until fully cooked and fairly dry; cool.
Knead maida with curd and water into a soft dough; rest 15 minutes.
Roll out, stuff with the cooked mince and seal.
Roast on a hot tawa with a little oil until golden with brown spots on both sides.
Serve hot with curd.
why_it_works: Non-vegetarian option within the soft, curd-leavened kulcha format, distinct from the vegetarian paneer and aloo versions
Lean mince keeps this high protein without excess fat
Same proven dough technique, different filling entirely

name: ZITLAS Chana Dal Khaman
description: A khaman made from ground chana dal instead of besan — a chunkier, higher-fiber variation on the classic spongy Gujarati steamed snack.
ingredients: Chana dal, soaked and ground — 120 g
instructions: Soak chana dal for at least 4 hours, grind with curd into a thick batter.
Add eno fruit salt just before steaming and mix gently.
Pour into a greased tin and steam for 12-15 minutes until well risen.
Cut into cubes, then temper mustard seeds and green chilli in oil and pour over the top.
why_it_works: Chana dal gives notably more protein and fiber than the refined besan version, with a slightly coarser bite
Same spongy steaming technique, genuinely different base pulse
Steamed, low added fat

name: ZITLAS Multigrain Thalipeeth
description: A thalipeeth made from a blend of five flours (jowar, bajra, ragi, besan, rice) — the most grain-diverse flatbread in the database, distinct from the three-flour standard Thalipeeth.
ingredients: Multigrain flour blend (jowar, bajra, ragi, besan, rice) — 70 g
instructions: Mix the multigrain flour blend with onion, cumin seeds, ajwain and enough water to form a soft dough.
Pat directly onto a hot, lightly oiled tawa into a thin round.
Poke a few holes, drizzle oil, and cook covered until golden on both sides.
Serve hot with curd.
why_it_works: Broadest grain blend of any thalipeeth in the database, spreading fiber and micronutrients across five sources rather than one to three
Same reliable hand-patting technique
Good grain-rotation option across the week

name: ZITLAS Roasted Poha Chivda
description: Dry roasted (not oil-tempered) poha tossed with peanuts and light spices — a genuinely different technique from the tempered kanda poha or oil-based chivda preparations elsewhere.
instructions: Dry-roast the thin poha in a wide kadai on low heat, stirring constantly, until crisp — this takes longer than tempering but uses no extra oil for the poha itself.
Separately, roast peanuts and curry leaves in a little oil with turmeric.
Toss the roasted poha with the peanut mixture.
Cool and store, or eat warm.
why_it_works: Dry-roasting the poha itself (rather than tempering it wet with oil and vegetables) is a genuinely different technique from every other poha preparation in the database
Can be stored for several days, unlike the fresh, wet kanda poha
Very low oil overall

name: ZITLAS Baked Vegetable Kachori
description: A whole wheat kachori filled with spiced mixed vegetables (not moong dal or paneer), baked — completing three distinct fillings for the baked-kachori format introduced in this batch.
instructions: Cook finely chopped vegetables with fennel seeds and coriander powder in a dry pan until soft and dry.
Knead atta with a little oil and water into a firm dough.
Roll small discs, stuff with the vegetable filling, seal and flatten gently.
Bake at 200°C for 18-20 minutes, turning once, until golden.
Serve with mint chutney.
why_it_works: Vegetable-only filling gives users a lower-protein, higher-fiber choice alongside the moong dal and paneer kachoris in this batch
Baked, not fried, keeping this meaningfully lighter
Good vegan option within the kachori family

name: ZITLAS Sabudana Khichu
description: A khichu made from sabudana instead of rice flour — a distinct fasting-day-style spoonable steamed-in-pan dish from the Moong Dal Khichu earlier in this batch.
instructions: Heat oil, temper cumin seeds and green chilli.
Add soaked sabudana, crushed peanuts and water, stirring continuously as it thickens and turns translucent, about 8-10 minutes.
Spoon into a bowl and eat with a spoon, while warm.
why_it_works: Sabudana's translucent, chewy texture is genuinely different from the smoother rice-moong khichu
Traditionally a fasting-day dish, reframed as a regular breakfast option
One-pot, minimal cleanup

name: ZITLAS Paneer Adai
description: Adai batter topped with crumbled paneer just before flipping — a protein-boosted adai variant distinct from the plain or vegetable versions.
instructions: Soak rice and dals for at least 4 hours, grind coarsely with red chilli and ginger.
Heat a tawa, pour a thick ladle of batter and spread into a coarse round.
Scatter crumbled paneer over the top while the first side cooks, pressing gently so it sticks.
Drizzle oil around the edges, flip carefully, and cook until crisp.
Serve hot with chutney.
why_it_works: Paneer topping raises the protein of an already high-protein multi-dal base even further
Distinct from the plain and vegetable adai variants by adding a dairy protein layer
Same reliable no-ferment technique

name: ZITLAS Vegetable Puttu Bowl
description: Steamed puttu crumbled into a bowl and tossed with a light vegetable stir-fry — a distinct serving format from the traditional cylindrical unmoulded puttu.
instructions: Prepare and steam puttu as usual with rice flour and grated coconut.
Heat oil, temper mustard seeds and curry leaves, then saute vegetables 3-4 minutes.
Crumble the steamed puttu into the pan and toss gently with the vegetables.
Serve warm in a bowl.
why_it_works: Crumbled-and-tossed bowl format is a genuinely different eating experience from the traditional unmoulded cylinder served plain
Vegetables add fiber and micronutrients not present in the plain version
Same steaming technique, different finishing

name: ZITLAS Egg Puttu Bowl
description: Steamed puttu crumbled and tossed with scrambled egg — a protein-added variant of the puttu family, distinct from the vegetable or plain versions.
instructions: Prepare and steam puttu as usual with rice flour and grated coconut.
Heat oil, saute onion, then scramble in the beaten egg until just cooked.
Crumble the steamed puttu into the pan and toss gently with the scrambled egg.
Serve warm in a bowl.
why_it_works: Egg addition meaningfully raises the protein of the traditionally protein-light puttu
Distinct texture combination — crumbly rice-coconut with soft scrambled egg
Same steaming technique, third distinct finishing in this batch

name: ZITLAS Fish Moilee Rice Bowl
description: A Kerala-style mild coconut-milk fish curry with curry leaves and turmeric, served over rice — a distinct regional fish preparation from the Bengali mustard-based fish curry already in the database.
ingredients: Curry leaves, turmeric, green chilli — 4 g
instructions: Heat oil, saute sliced onion until soft, add curry leaves, turmeric and green chilli.
Add coconut milk and a little water, bring to a gentle simmer.
Add the fish and simmer for 6-8 minutes until just cooked through, without stirring too much so it doesn't break apart.
Serve the curry over warm rice.
why_it_works: Coconut milk and curry leaves give a distinctly mild, creamy Kerala flavour profile, genuinely different from the mustard-and-panch-phoron Bengali fish curry already in the database
Gentle simmering keeps the fish tender
Third distinct regional fish preparation, broadening non-vegetarian variety

name: ZITLAS Prawn Cutlet Sandwich
description: Pan-fried prawn cutlets sandwiched in toasted bread — a distinct seafood-based cutlet-sandwich format from the fish cutlet sandwich already in the database.
ingredients: Ginger, green chilli, black pepper — 5 g
instructions: Finely chop the prawns and mix with onion, ginger, green chilli and black pepper.
Shape into a flat cutlet.
Pan-fry in oil until golden and firm on both sides, about 3-4 minutes per side.

Refrigerate overnight.
Stir again and eat cold in the morning.

instructions: Pressure cook toor dal until soft.
Heat oil, temper with goda masala, then add the cooked dal, kokum and a little jaggery, along with water to loosen.
Simmer 8-10 minutes to let the flavours combine.
Serve hot over rice.
why_it_works: Goda masala and kokum give amti a distinctly sweet-sour-spicy profile, genuinely different from the plain Varan or any North Indian dal in the database
Kolhapuri specialty, more complex in flavour than everyday varan
Same base legume, deliberately different technique and seasoning

name: ZITLAS Bharli Vangi with Bhakri
description: Baby eggplants stuffed with a spiced peanut-coconut masala and simmered, served with bhakri — a distinct stuffed-vegetable curry technique not used anywhere else in the database.
instructions: Knead jowar flour into a bhakri and cook on a tawa.
Slit the baby brinjals lengthwise without cutting through, keeping the stem intact.
Mix ground peanuts, grated coconut and goda masala into a thick stuffing paste, and fill each brinjal.
Heat oil in a kadai, place the stuffed brinjals in, add a little water, cover and simmer 15-18 minutes until tender.
Serve hot with the bhakri.
why_it_works: The peanut-coconut stuffing technique is genuinely distinct from any other vegetable preparation in the database
Whole stuffed baby eggplants rather than chopped vegetable is a different cooking approach entirely
Iconic Maharashtrian festive dish reframed as an everyday lunch

name: ZITLAS Kolhapuri Pandhra Rassa Chicken Bowl
description: A mild, white coconut-based Kolhapuri chicken curry — one half of the famous Kolhapuri rassa pair, distinctly milder than its red counterpart.
ingredients: Whole spices (no red chilli), poppy seeds — 5 g
instructions: Grind grated coconut with poppy seeds and a little water into a smooth white paste.
Heat oil, saute onion until soft (without browning too much, to keep the gravy pale), add whole spices.
Add the chicken and cook 5 minutes, then stir in the coconut paste and water; simmer 15-18 minutes until the chicken is tender.
Serve hot, deliberately mild and creamy rather than spicy.
why_it_works: Pandhra rassa's defining feature is its mildness and pale colour, achieved by avoiding red chilli and browning — a genuinely distinct technique from every other chicken curry in the database
Traditionally served alongside the spicy tambda rassa as a cooling contrast
Coconut-poppy seed base gives real textural richness without excess oil

name: ZITLAS Kolhapuri Tambda Rassa Chicken Bowl
description: A fiery red Kolhapuri chicken curry, the spicier counterpart to the pandhra rassa in this batch — deep red from a specific dried-chilli paste, genuinely distinct in both colour and heat.
ingredients: Dried Kolhapuri red chillies, ground — 8 g
instructions: Deep-fry or dry-roast the sliced onion until dark golden, then blend with dried Kolhapuri chillies, garlic, ginger and a little coconut into a thick, deep red paste.
Heat oil, add the paste and cook until the oil separates.
Add the chicken and water, and simmer 18-20 minutes until tender and the gravy is deep red and thick.
Serve hot — this is deliberately the spicier, more intense curry of the Kolhapuri pair.
why_it_works: The specific dried-chilli paste and deep-fried onion base are what give tambda rassa its famous heat and colour, genuinely different from the mild pandhra rassa in this batch
One of India's most famous fiery curries, offering real spice-level variety for users who want it
The two rassa recipes are traditionally served together, so both are included as a legitimate pair

name: ZITLAS Malvani Fish Curry Rice Bowl
description: A spicy, coconut-and-kokum-based Malvani fish curry from the Konkan coast — distinct from the milder Bengali, Kerala or Assamese fish curries already in the database.
instructions: Grind grated coconut with Malvani masala and garlic into a thick red paste.
Heat oil, add the paste and cook until fragrant.
Add water and kokum, bring to a simmer, then gently add the fish and cook 6-8 minutes until just cooked through.
Serve over warm rice.
why_it_works: Malvani masala's specific spice blend and kokum's tang give this a genuinely distinct flavour profile from every other fish curry in the database
Konkan coastal cooking style, spicier and more coconut-forward than the Kerala or Bengali versions already represented
Kokum instead of tamarind or lemon as the souring agent is a regionally specific choice

name: ZITLAS Malvani Prawn Sukka
description: A dry, intensely spiced prawn preparation from the Konkan coast — distinct from the wet Prawn Curry Rice Bowl and Prawn Biryani already in the database by its dry, coconut-coated texture.
instructions: Heat oil, saute onion until golden.
Add Malvani masala and grated coconut, roasting for 2-3 minutes until fragrant.
Add the prawns and cook on medium-high heat for 5-6 minutes, tossing continuously, until the prawns are cooked and the mixture is dry, not saucy.
Serve hot as a dry side with rice or bhakri.
why_it_works: Sukka's dry, coconut-coated technique is genuinely different from the wet-gravy prawn preparations already in the database
Prawns cook very fast, so this dry method concentrates flavour quickly without a long simmer
Distinct texture — clingy and roasted, not saucy

name: ZITLAS Kombdi Sukka
description: Dry, deeply roasted spiced chicken with coconut — a distinct dry-preparation technique from the wet Kolhapuri rassa curries already in this batch.
instructions: Heat oil, saute onion until deep golden.
Add masala and grated coconut, roasting until fragrant.
Add the chicken and a small splash of water, cover and cook 18-20 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the chicken is tender and the mixture has dried down and roasted.
Serve as a dry side dish.
why_it_works: Dry sukka technique is genuinely different from the wet gravy of the pandhra and tambda rassa already in this batch, giving users a textural choice for the same protein
Roasted coconut coating concentrates flavour without a thin gravy
Traditional accompaniment to bhakri

name: ZITLAS Matki Chi Usal Lunchbox Bowl
description: A dry-cooked sprouted matki usal specifically thickened and reduced so it travels well in a lunchbox for several hours — distinct from the breakfast-format Matki Usal Bowl by its consistency and purpose.
instructions: Heat oil, saute onion until golden, add goda masala.
Add boiled matki with only a small splash of water, and cook down until thick and dry rather than saucy, about 10-12 minutes — this dryness is what makes it travel well.
Pack while warm into a lunchbox.
Eat within a few hours, at room temperature or reheated.
why_it_works: Deliberately dry-cooked (unlike a home-eaten wet usal) so it doesn't leak or spoil as fast in a packed lunchbox
Designed specifically around the office/college lunchbox constraint rather than immediate home eating
High protein and fiber for a sustained afternoon

name: ZITLAS Val (Lilva Beans) Usal Bowl
description: A tempered curry made from val (field beans) — introducing a legume not used anywhere else in the database, prepared usal-style.
instructions: Heat oil, saute onion and garlic until golden, add goda masala.
Add boiled val beans with a little water and simmer 8-10 minutes.
Serve hot with rice or bhakri.
why_it_works: Val (field beans) is a genuinely new legume for the database, with a distinct earthy flavour from moong, chana or matki
Winter-season Maharashtrian legume, adding real seasonal and nutritional variety
Same reliable usal technique applied to a new pulse

name: ZITLAS Masoor Usal Bowl
description: A tempered masoor dal usal — a distinct legume choice from the moong, matki, chana, or val usals already used in the database.
ingredients: Masoor dal, boiled (whole, not split) — 130 g
instructions: Heat oil, saute onion until golden, add goda masala.
Add boiled whole masoor and a little water, simmering 6-8 minutes.
Serve hot with rice or bhakri.
why_it_works: Whole masoor (not split red lentil) is a distinct legume choice from any usal already in the database
Quick-cooking compared to matki or val, good for a faster lunch
Same reliable usal technique, different pulse each time

name: ZITLAS Alu Panchamrut Vegetable Bowl
description: A five-vegetable Maharashtrian curry combining brinjal, potato, beans and other seasonal vegetables in a single spiced gravy — a distinct multi-vegetable combination dish.
instructions: Heat oil, temper with goda masala.
Add all the vegetables together and saute 3-4 minutes.
Add a little water and simmer 15-18 minutes until all vegetables are tender.
Stir in crushed peanuts for texture and protein.
Serve hot with bhakri or rice.
why_it_works: Combining five distinct vegetables in one pot is a genuinely different composition from any single-vegetable curry in the database
Peanuts stirred in at the end add protein and crunch not usually found in a mixed-vegetable sabzi
Traditional Maharashtrian technique of building flavour across multiple vegetables at once

name: ZITLAS Zunka Bhakri Family Thali
description: A larger, thali-format version of zunka bhakri with sides of curd, salad and pickle — a shared family meal format distinct from the individual breakfast bowl already in the database.
instructions: Make three bhakris from the jowar flour, cooking each on a hot tawa.
Prepare a larger batch of zunka as in the breakfast version, scaled up for three servings.
Plate as a thali with the bhakris, zunka, and simple sides like sliced onion or curd.
Serve family-style for sharing.
why_it_works: Scaled for sharing across a family rather than a single portion, a genuinely different meal-planning purpose from the individual breakfast bowl
Thali format with sides changes the eating experience from a simple bowl
Same core recipe, different serving context and scale

name: ZITLAS Soya Chi Bhaji with Bhakri
description: Soya chunks cooked in a Maharashtrian-style onion-tomato gravy with goda masala, served with bhakri — a distinct regional treatment of soya from the keema, frankie or biryani preparations already in the database.
instructions: Knead jowar flour into a bhakri and cook on a tawa.
Heat oil, saute onion and tomato until soft, add goda masala.
Add the rehydrated soya chunks and a little water; simmer 8-10 minutes.
Serve hot with the bhakri.
why_it_works: Goda masala's specific sweet-spicy blend gives this soya preparation a genuinely different flavour direction from the keema, frankie or biryani soya recipes already in the database
Bhakri pairing (not roti or rice) is a distinctly Maharashtrian meal structure
High protein, budget-friendly

name: ZITLAS Maharashtrian Kadhi Bhaat Bowl
description: A besan-and-curd kadhi with a distinctly Maharashtrian sweet-and-mild spice profile, served over rice — different from the tangier Gujarati-style Besan Kadhi Bowl already in the database.
ingredients: Jaggery, mustard seeds, curry leaves — 5 g
instructions: Whisk besan into curd and water until smooth.
Heat oil, temper mustard seeds and curry leaves.
Pour in the besan-curd mixture, add a small piece of jaggery, and simmer gently, stirring often, for 10-12 minutes until thickened.
Serve over warm rice.
why_it_works: A touch of jaggery gives Maharashtrian kadhi a distinctly milder, slightly sweet profile compared to the tangier Gujarati kadhi already in the database
Curd base provides real protein
Comforting, easy-to-digest lunch

name: ZITLAS Vangi Bhaat
description: A one-pot eggplant-and-rice dish flavoured with goda masala — a distinct rice preparation from any pulao or biryani already in the database.
instructions: Heat oil, temper whole spices, add brinjal and peanuts, and saute 3-4 minutes.
Add rice and goda masala, mixing well.
Add water in the standard ratio and pressure cook for 2 whistles.
Fluff with a fork and serve hot.
why_it_works: Goda masala's specific sweet-spicy Maharashtrian blend distinguishes this from any other spiced rice dish in the database
Brinjal cooked directly into the rice, not as a separate side
One-pot, mostly hands-off preparation

name: ZITLAS Masale Bhaat
description: A spiced mixed-vegetable rice using goda masala and a wider vegetable mix than Vangi Bhaat, without eggplant as the dominant flavour — a distinct one-pot rice preparation from this batch's other rice dishes.
instructions: Heat oil, temper whole spices, add mixed vegetables and saute 3-4 minutes.
Add rice and goda masala, mixing well.
Add water in the standard ratio and pressure cook for 2 whistles.
Fluff with a fork and serve hot.
why_it_works: Uses a broader vegetable mix rather than being built around one dominant vegetable like the Vangi Bhaat in this batch
Same goda masala base but a genuinely different vegetable composition and flavour balance
Family-friendly, less intensely flavoured than vangi bhaat

name: ZITLAS Portion-Controlled Puran Poli with Protein Kadhi
description: A single small puran poli (sweet stuffed flatbread) paired specifically with a protein-rich kadhi side to balance the meal — a portion-controlled way to enjoy a traditionally rich festive sweet.
ingredients: Chana dal, cooked and mashed — 50 g
instructions: Cook mashed chana dal with jaggery into a thick, dry filling (puran).
Roll a small ball of atta dough thin, place a portion of puran in the centre, seal and roll out gently into a thin flatbread.
Cook on a hot tawa until lightly browned on both sides.
Separately whisk curd with besan and water, and simmer into a light kadhi.
Serve one small puran poli alongside a generous bowl of kadhi to balance the meal with protein.
why_it_works: Deliberately single, small-portion puran poli paired with a protein-forward kadhi, rather than multiple polis eaten alone, balances the traditionally rich sweet with real protein
Chana dal filling itself contributes some protein, unlike a purely sugar-based sweet
Festive dish made into a considered, portion-aware everyday meal

name: ZITLAS Konkan Fish Thali Bowl
description: A multi-component Konkan meal combining rice, a small fish curry portion, and a side of solkadhi — a distinct thali format bringing together several Konkan elements in one balanced bowl.
instructions: Cook a small portion of fish curry using coconut milk, kokum and Malvani masala, simmering the fish gently for 6-8 minutes.
Separately mix a little coconut milk with kokum water to make a small side of solkadhi.
Serve the fish curry over rice with the solkadhi alongside as a palate-cleansing drink.
why_it_works: Combining a curry, rice and a drink side into one considered thali is a genuinely different meal structure from a single fish-curry-and-rice bowl
Solkadhi traditionally aids digestion after a coconut-heavy meal, a purposeful pairing rather than a random addition
Represents a complete, authentic Konkan meal structure rather than one isolated dish

name: ZITLAS Chicken Kolhapuri Lunchbox Wrap
description: Kolhapuri-spiced shredded chicken wrapped in a roti, engineered specifically to hold together and travel for an office lunchbox — distinct from eating the same curry as a bowl at home.
ingredients: Chicken, lean, shredded after cooking — 100 g
instructions: Cook the chicken in oil with Kolhapuri masala until fully done, then shred it and cook down any liquid until the mixture is dry rather than saucy (this is what makes it travel well).
Roll out and roast the atta into a roti.
Spread the dry, spiced shredded chicken onto the roti with sliced onion, and roll tightly.
Wrap in foil — it holds together for several hours without leaking.
why_it_works: Deliberately dry-cooked and shredded (unlike the saucy Kolhapuri rassa curries in this batch) specifically so it works as a portable wrap
Kolhapuri spice intensity carries well even without a wet gravy
Designed around the actual constraint of an office lunchbox rather than home eating

name: ZITLAS Kolhapuri Mutton Rassa Bowl
description: A rich, spiced Kolhapuri mutton curry — introducing mutton in a genuine Kolhapuri preparation, distinct from the plainer Lean Mutton Curry Rice Bowl already in the database.
ingredients: Dried Kolhapuri red chillies, ground — 8 g
instructions: Fry sliced onion until deep golden, then blend with dried Kolhapuri chillies, garlic, ginger and coconut into a thick paste.
Heat oil, add the paste and cook until the oil separates.
Add the mutton and enough water to cover, then pressure cook for 15-18 minutes until tender.
Serve hot, deliberately spicy and deep red.
why_it_works: Kolhapuri masala's specific dried-chilli paste gives this a genuinely distinct regional identity from the simpler home-style mutton curry already in the database
Pressure cooking keeps mutton's usually long cooking time practical
One of Maharashtra's most iconic non-vegetarian dishes

name: ZITLAS Malvani Chicken Curry Bowl
description: A coconut-forward Konkan chicken curry, distinct from the drier Kombdi Sukka in this batch and the Kolhapuri rassa curries by its specific coastal spice blend.
instructions: Grind grated coconut with Malvani masala into a thick paste.
Heat oil, saute onion until golden, add the coconut paste and cook until fragrant.
Add the chicken and water, and simmer 18-20 minutes until tender.
Serve hot with rice or bhakri.
why_it_works: Malvani masala's coastal spice blend, heavier on coconut, is genuinely distinct from the deep-fried-onion-based Kolhapuri curries in this batch
Wet, saucy format distinct from the dry Kombdi Sukka
Konkan coastal identity, different from the inland Kolhapur style

name: ZITLAS Baked Bombil (Bombay Duck) Bowl
description: Bombil, the iconic Mumbai fish, coated in a light spiced batter and baked instead of the traditional deep-fry — introducing a distinct fish species not used anywhere else in the database.
ingredients: Turmeric, red chilli powder, semolina — 6 g
instructions: Marinate the bombil fillets with turmeric and red chilli powder.
Coat lightly in a mix of rice flour and semolina.
Arrange on a lightly oiled tray and bake at 200°C for 12-15 minutes, turning once, until crisp and cooked through.
Serve hot with a wedge of lemon.
why_it_works: Bombil (Bombay duck) is a genuinely distinct, delicate fish species iconic to Mumbai, not used anywhere else in the database
Baking instead of deep-frying keeps this meaningfully lighter than the traditional street-food preparation
Rice flour and semolina coating gives a crisp texture without the usual oil load

name: ZITLAS Surmai (Kingfish) Curry Rice Bowl
description: A Konkan-style curry using surmai (kingfish), a firmer, meatier fish than the lean fillets used elsewhere in the database — a distinct fish species and texture.
instructions: Heat oil, add Malvani masala and cook briefly.
Add coconut milk and a little water, bring to a simmer.
Add the surmai steak and cook gently for 8-10 minutes, turning once, until just cooked through (kingfish holds together better than delicate fillets).
Serve over warm rice.
why_it_works: Surmai's firm, meaty texture is genuinely different from the flakier lean fish used in every other fish curry in the database
A prized, popular Konkan fish offering real variety for non-vegetarian users
Holds its shape well through cooking, a distinct textural experience

name: ZITLAS Kolhapuri-Style Egg Curry Bowl
description: Boiled eggs simmered in a Kolhapuri masala gravy — distinct from the Nagpuri saoji, Bengali, Chettinad or standard egg curries already in the database by its specific dried-chilli paste base.
ingredients: Dried Kolhapuri red chillies, ground — 6 g
instructions: Fry sliced onion until golden, blend with dried Kolhapuri chillies, garlic and coconut into a paste.
Heat oil, cook the paste until the oil separates.
Add water to form a gravy and simmer 8-10 minutes.
Halve the boiled eggs and simmer in the gravy for 3-4 minutes.
Serve hot.
why_it_works: Kolhapuri masala's specific dried-chilli base gives this a genuinely different flavour identity from the Nagpuri saoji or Bengali panch-phoron egg curries already in the database
Same reliable curry technique used for chicken and mutton in this batch, applied to eggs for a budget-friendly protein option
Deep red, spicy Kolhapuri character

name: ZITLAS Soya Kolhapuri Bowl
description: Soya chunks cooked in a Kolhapuri-style spiced gravy — a vegetarian option using the same distinctive Kolhapuri paste as the meat and egg curries in this batch.
ingredients: Dried Kolhapuri red chillies, ground — 6 g
instructions: Fry sliced onion until golden, blend with dried Kolhapuri chillies, garlic and coconut into a paste.
Heat oil, cook the paste until fragrant.
Add the rehydrated soya chunks and water; simmer 10-12 minutes.
Serve hot with rice or bhakri.
why_it_works: Gives vegetarian and vegan users access to the same distinctive Kolhapuri flavour profile as the meat and egg versions in this batch
High protein, budget-friendly alternative to the meat curries
Same fiery regional character, different protein base

name: ZITLAS Paneer Kolhapuri Bowl
description: Paneer cubes simmered in Kolhapuri masala — a dairy-protein option within the same Kolhapuri flavour family as the soya, egg, chicken and mutton versions in this batch.
ingredients: Dried Kolhapuri red chillies, ground — 6 g
instructions: Fry sliced onion until golden, blend with dried Kolhapuri chillies, garlic and coconut into a paste.
Heat oil, cook the paste until fragrant.
Add water to form a gravy, then gently add the paneer cubes and simmer 5-6 minutes (avoid overcooking so the paneer stays soft).
Serve hot with rice or bhakri.
why_it_works: Completes the set of five distinct proteins (mutton, chicken, egg, soya, paneer) sharing the same Kolhapuri flavour base in this batch, letting users choose by preference or budget
Paneer's mild flavour absorbs the fiery masala well
Familiar protein in a genuinely regional preparation

name: ZITLAS Tofu Malvani Bowl
description: Tofu simmered in a coconut-based Malvani gravy — a vegan protein option using the Konkan coastal flavour profile rather than the inland Kolhapuri base used elsewhere in this batch.
instructions: Grind grated coconut with Malvani masala into a paste.
Heat oil, saute onion, add the coconut paste and cook until fragrant.
Add water to form a gravy, then gently add the tofu cubes and simmer 6-8 minutes.
Serve hot with rice.
why_it_works: Uses the Malvani (coastal) flavour profile rather than the Kolhapuri (inland) base used for the other proteins in this batch, giving genuine regional variety within Maharashtra itself
Fully vegan, high protein
Coconut-forward gravy pairs well with tofu's mild flavour

name: ZITLAS Chawli Usal Dinner Bowl
description: A tempered curry made from cooked cowpea (chawli), prepared usal-style — a warm, cooked dinner preparation distinct from the raw salad and cooked-roll uses of the same legume already in the database.
instructions: Heat oil, saute onion until golden, add goda masala.
Add boiled chawli with a little water and simmer 8-10 minutes.
Serve hot with bhakri or rice.
why_it_works: Usal preparation (tempered, moderately dry) gives chawli a third genuinely distinct role in the database, alongside its raw salad and gravy-roll uses
Goda masala ties this into the same Maharashtrian usal family as the matki, val and masoor versions
Warm, simple dinner preparation

name: ZITLAS Bhakri with Pithla Light Dinner
description: A lighter, dinner-portioned pithla and bhakri combination specifically kept smaller and less oily than the breakfast version — framed around an early, light evening meal.
instructions: Knead jowar flour into a smaller bhakri and cook on a tawa.
Heat oil, temper cumin seeds and garlic.
Whisk besan with water into a thin batter and pour in, stirring until it thickens into a smooth gravy.
Serve a modest portion hot with the bhakri — deliberately lighter than a full breakfast serving.
why_it_works: Deliberately smaller portions and less oil than the breakfast Pithla Bhakri Bowl already in the database, appropriate for a lighter evening meal
Same core dish, different portioning philosophy for a different time of day
Easy to digest before sleep

name: ZITLAS Malvani Prawns Curry Bowl
description: A wet, coconut-based Malvani prawn curry — the saucy counterpart to the dry Malvani Prawn Sukka in this batch's lunch section, giving users a textural choice for the same protein.
instructions: Grind grated coconut with Malvani masala into a paste.
Heat oil, saute onion, add the coconut paste and cook until fragrant.
Add water to form a gravy, then add the prawns and simmer just 4-5 minutes until pink and cooked through.
Serve over rice.
why_it_works: Wet, saucy format is a deliberate contrast to the dry Malvani Prawn Sukka in this batch's lunch section, giving genuine textural choice for the same protein and region
Prawns cook fast, keeping this a realistically quick dinner despite the gravy
Classic Konkan coastal preparation

name: ZITLAS Vidarbha-Style Chicken Rassa Bowl
description: A Vidarbha-region chicken curry with its own distinct spice character, separate from the Kolhapuri pandhra and tambda rassa already in this batch — offering a third regional Maharashtrian chicken curry style.
ingredients: Dry-roasted whole spices (coriander, sesame, dried chilli) — 6 g
instructions: Dry-roast whole spices including sesame seeds, then grind to a coarse powder.
Heat oil, saute onion until golden, add garlic, ginger and the roasted spice powder.
Add the chicken and water, and simmer 18-20 minutes until tender.
Serve hot with bhakri or rice.
why_it_works: Vidarbha's dry-roasted whole-spice technique, including sesame, gives a genuinely different flavour base from the coconut-heavy Kolhapuri or Malvani curries in this batch
Third distinct Maharashtrian regional chicken curry style represented, alongside Kolhapur and Konkan
Nagpur-Vidarbha cuisine known for its bold, complex spicing

name: ZITLAS Sprouted Matki Amti Bowl
description: Sprouted matki cooked in a tangy, kokum-soured amti gravy — a distinct preparation from the plain Matki Usal already in the database by its sourness and gravy consistency.
instructions: Heat oil, saute onion until golden, add goda masala.
Add boiled matki, kokum and a little jaggery, along with water to form a gravy; simmer 10-12 minutes.
Serve hot with rice or bhakri.
why_it_works: Kokum's souring gives this a genuinely different, tangier profile from the plain, less-sour Matki Usal Bowl already in the database
Amti's sweet-sour-spicy balance is a distinctly Maharashtrian approach to legume cookery
Same base legume, different, more complex preparation

name: ZITLAS Paneer Bharli Vangi-Style Stuffed Capsicum
description: The peanut-coconut stuffing technique from Bharli Vangi adapted into capsicum with paneer added for extra protein — a distinct vessel and protein combination from the original eggplant version.
instructions: Mix ground peanuts, grated coconut, crumbled paneer and goda masala into a thick stuffing.
Fill the capsicum halves with the mixture.
Heat oil in a kadai, place the stuffed capsicum in, add a little water, cover and simmer 15-18 minutes until the capsicum softens.
Serve hot.
why_it_works: Adapts the distinctive Bharli Vangi peanut-coconut stuffing technique to a different vessel and adds paneer, giving a genuinely higher-protein variant of the original eggplant dish
Two protein sources combined directly in the stuffing
Capsicum cooks faster than whole eggplant, making this a quicker dinner option

name: ZITLAS Solkadhi and Rice Light Dinner Bowl
description: A small portion of rice paired with solkadhi as a light, easily digestible dinner — distinct from the breakfast Solkadhi and Roasted Chana Combo by being a warm-rice pairing rather than a cold drink-and-snack combo.
instructions: Soak kokum in a little warm water.
Whisk the kokum water into coconut milk with garlic and cumin.
Pour the solkadhi over warm rice in a bowl, like a thin, tangy soup-rice combination.
Eat immediately while the rice is still warm.
why_it_works: Rice-and-solkadhi pairing is a traditional light-dinner combination, distinct from the drink-and-snack breakfast pairing already in the database
Very light and easy to digest before sleep
Minimal cooking required

name: ZITLAS Steamed Rice Dumplings with Soya Keema Filling
description: A modak-shaped steamed dumpling filled with spiced soya keema instead of the moong filling used in the breakfast version — a distinct protein filling for the same traditional shape.
ingredients: Soya chunks, rehydrated and finely chopped — 70 g
instructions: Knead rice flour with boiling water into a smooth dough.
Cook the finely chopped soya chunks with ginger-garlic paste and garam masala until well spiced and slightly dry.
Shape small discs of dough, pleat the edges, fill with the soya keema, and gather into the traditional modak shape.
Steam in a pressure cooker (without the whistle) for 12-15 minutes.
Serve warm.
why_it_works: Soya keema filling gives notably more protein than the moong-filled breakfast version, better suited to a muscle-gain-focused dinner
Same distinctive pleated shape and steaming technique, different protein purpose
Higher protein density for an evening meal

name: ZITLAS Bhakri Pizza-Style Zunka Topped
description: A jowar bhakri spread with zunka and topped with vegetables, briefly grilled — a playful, family-friendly presentation distinct from serving zunka and bhakri as two separate components.
instructions: Cook two bhakris on a tawa as usual.
Prepare zunka as normal with besan, turmeric and mustard seeds.
Spread the zunka thickly over each bhakri and scatter chopped vegetables on top.
Return to the tawa briefly, covered, to warm through and soften the vegetables slightly.
Slice like a pizza and serve.
why_it_works: Combining zunka and bhakri into a single topped, sliced format is a genuinely different presentation from serving them as two separate components
Family-friendly, fun way to get kids interested in a traditional dish
Same core ingredients, different construction

name: ZITLAS Family-Style Masale Bhaat Platter
description: A larger-batch version of Masale Bhaat with added paneer and a wider vegetable mix, plated as a shared family platter — distinct from the individual lunch portion already in this batch.
instructions: Heat oil, temper whole spices, add mixed vegetables and saute 4-5 minutes.
Add rice, goda masala and paneer cubes, mixing gently.
Add water in the standard ratio and pressure cook for 2-3 whistles.
Fluff gently (to avoid breaking the paneer) and serve family-style on a large platter.
why_it_works: Paneer addition and larger batch size make this a genuinely different meal-planning purpose from the individual lunch Masale Bhaat in this batch — a shared family dinner rather than a solo lunch
Higher protein than the lunch version thanks to the paneer

name: ZITLAS Kanda Chutney Roti Roll

Blend onion with dried red chilli, garlic and roasted peanuts into a coarse, pungent chutney.
Spread the chutney generously onto the roti and roll tightly.
Serve immediately (best eaten fresh, as raw onion chutney doesn't keep well).
why_it_works: Using a pungent raw chutney as the primary filling, rather than a cooked curry or vegetable, is a genuinely different meal concept from any other roll in the database

name: ZITLAS Marathwada Ras Bhaji Combo
description: A thin, spiced vegetable broth (ras) served alongside a dry vegetable side (bhaji) — a distinct two-component meal structure specific to Marathwada, different from a single curry-and-rice bowl.
instructions: Cook half the vegetables into a thin, well-spiced broth (ras) with ground peanuts, tamarind and plenty of water, simmering 15 minutes.
Separately, stir-fry the remaining vegetables dry with a little oil and goda masala as the bhaji side.
Serve the ras in a bowl alongside the dry bhaji, eaten together with bhakri.
why_it_works: The deliberate two-component structure — a thin broth and a separate dry vegetable — is a genuinely different meal format from a single unified curry already in the database
Specific to Marathwada's distinctive way of structuring a vegetable meal
Peanuts in the ras supply protein

name: ZITLAS Vidarbha-Style Bharda
description: A smoky roasted eggplant-tomato-garlic mash with a distinctive Vidarbha spice blend — genuinely different from the plain Vangyache Bharit Toast already in the database by its tomato-garlic base and dinner-portioned bhakri pairing.
instructions: Knead jowar flour into a bhakri and cook on a tawa.
Roast the eggplant, tomato and garlic together directly over a flame until charred and soft.
Peel and mash everything together into a smoky, garlicky mash.
Heat a little oil and quickly temper the mash.
Serve hot with the bhakri.
why_it_works: Adding roasted tomato and garlic to the mash gives this a genuinely different flavour base from the plain Vangyache Bharit already in the database, and Vidarbha's spicing makes it distinctly bolder
Smoky, open-flame technique preserved from the breakfast version but built into a heartier dinner combination
Rustic, authentically regional

name: ZITLAS Sindhudurg Coconut Rice Bowl
description: Rice simmered in coconut milk with a light tempering — a simple, mild coastal rice preparation distinct from the spiced vangi bhaat, masale bhaat or biryani-style rice dishes already in the database.
instructions: Heat oil, temper mustard seeds and curry leaves, lightly roast the cashews.
Add rice, coconut milk and water in place of some of the water, then pressure cook for 2 whistles.
Fluff and serve hot.
why_it_works: Deliberately mild and coconut-forward, distinct from the goda-masala-heavy vangi bhaat or masale bhaat already in the database
Cashews (a Sindhudurg coastal crop) add protein and richness
Simple, comforting coastal home food

name: ZITLAS Kaju Konkan Curry Bowl
description: Cashews (a major Sindhudurg and Konkan crop) simmered in a light coconut gravy as the primary protein — a distinct nut-as-main-ingredient dish not resembling any other recipe in the database.
instructions: Heat oil, saute onion until soft, add Malvani masala.
Add coconut milk and a little water, bring to a gentle simmer.
Add whole cashews and simmer 8-10 minutes until they soften slightly but retain some bite.
Serve with rice.
why_it_works: Cashews used as the star protein-and-texture ingredient, rather than a garnish, is a genuinely unique concept not resembling any other dish in the database
Konkan is one of India's major cashew-growing regions, making this a genuinely regional specialty
Rich, satisfying, distinct nutty-creamy texture

name: ZITLAS Ratnagiri Grilled Fish Bowl
description: Fish marinated in a light Konkan spice paste and grilled — a distinct cooking technique (grilled, not curried or pan-fried) from every other fish preparation already in the database.
instructions: Marinate the fish in curd, Malvani masala and turmeric for at least 15 minutes.
Grill in an oven or air fryer at 200°C for 10-12 minutes, turning once, until charred at the edges and cooked through.
Serve with lemon wedges.
why_it_works: Grilling is a genuinely different technique from the curry (Malvani, Kolhapuri), sukka (dry-roasted with coconut) or baked-and-coated preparations already used for fish in the database
Curd marinade tenderizes without adding much fat
Clean, direct flavour without a heavy gravy

name: ZITLAS Alu Chi Dandi Bhaji
description: Colocasia (arbi) stems cooked into a tangy sabzi — using a different part of the plant from the leaves used in Alu Vadi, a genuinely distinct vegetable preparation.
instructions: Heat oil, temper turmeric.
Add chopped colocasia stems and tamarind, cover and simmer 15-18 minutes until tender (the tamarind neutralizes the stem's natural itchiness).
Stir in crushed peanuts.
Serve with bhakri or rice.
why_it_works: Using the stems rather than the leaves of the colocasia plant (already used for Alu Vadi) is a genuinely different vegetable choice with a distinct crunchy-then-tender texture
Tamarind's souring is specifically necessary to neutralize the stem's natural irritant quality, a real technique detail
Resourceful, traditional use of the whole plant

name: ZITLAS Leftover Amti Rice Cutlets
description: Leftover amti (dal) and rice mashed together with a besan binder and pan-fried into cutlets — a genuinely different leftover-rescue technique from the poha- or roti-based leftover recipes already in the database.
instructions: Mash leftover amti and rice together with besan and chilli powder until it holds together (drain excess liquid from the amti first if very thin).
Shape into small cutlets.
Pan-fry in oil until crisp and golden on both sides.
Serve with chutney.
why_it_works: Specifically rescues leftover amti — a wet dal — combined with rice, a genuinely different leftover pairing from any other leftover-rescue recipe already in the database
Besan binds two otherwise-wet leftovers into a cookable shape
Reduces food waste from a very commonly leftover dish

name: ZITLAS Paneer Bhopla Bhaji Dinner Bowl
description: Pumpkin cooked with paneer added for extra protein — a dinner-portioned, protein-boosted variant of the breakfast Bhoplyachi Bhaji already in this collection.
instructions: Heat oil, temper mustard seeds and turmeric.
Add cubed pumpkin and a little water, cover and cook 10-12 minutes until soft.
Gently stir in paneer cubes and warm through for 2-3 minutes.
Serve with rice or bhakri.
why_it_works: Paneer addition gives this notably more protein than the breakfast pumpkin bhaji already in this collection, better suited to a muscle-gain-focused dinner

name: ZITLAS Post-Workout Fish Amti Bowl
description: Fish cooked in a tangy kokum amti-style gravy over rice, specifically timed and portioned for after an evening workout — a seafood counterpart to the soya and chicken post-workout amti bowls already in the database.
instructions: Heat oil, temper with goda masala.
Add kokum and water to form a light gravy, bring to a simmer.
Add the fish and cook gently 6-8 minutes until just cooked through.
Serve over rice within 45-60 minutes of finishing an evening workout.
why_it_works: Fish cooks fast and is a complete, lean protein, making this a genuinely practical post-workout option alongside the soya and chicken amti versions already in the database

name: ZITLAS Family-Style Suran Bhaji Platter
description: A larger-batch version of the Suran Bhaji Bowl with added peanuts and a wider spice profile, plated for sharing — distinct from the individual lunch portion by scale and richer seasoning.
instructions: Heat oil, saute onion until golden, add goda masala.
Add cubed suran, ground peanuts and a little water, cover and simmer 18-20 minutes until tender.
Stir in tamarind for tang.
Serve family-style on a large platter with rice or bhakri for three people to share.
why_it_works: Peanuts added and scaled for sharing make this a genuinely different meal-planning purpose from the individual lunch Suran Bhaji Bowl already in this collection
Higher protein per portion than the lunch version thanks to the peanuts
Good way to introduce a family to an underused vegetable

name: ZITLAS Baked Karle Chips Snack
description: Bitter gourd sliced thin and baked into crisp chips — a genuinely different vegetable-chip format from any potato- or besan-based snack already in the database.
instructions: Slice the bitter gourd very thin and toss with a little salt; let sit 10 minutes to draw out excess moisture, then pat dry.
Toss with oil and turmeric.
Arrange in a single layer on a tray and bake at 180°C for 18-20 minutes, turning once, until crisp.
Cool before eating for maximum crunch.
why_it_works: Baked vegetable chip format is a genuinely different snack category from any potato- or besan-based snack in the database
Thin slicing and salting reduces bitterness naturally without deep-frying
Very low calorie, high volume

name: ZITLAS Baked Suran Chips Snack
description: Yam sliced thin and baked into crisp chips — a distinct vegetable-chip base from the Baked Karle Chips in this batch, with a starchier, denser bite.
instructions: Slice the yam very thin.
Toss with oil, red chilli powder and salt.
Arrange in a single layer on a tray and bake at 190°C for 18-20 minutes, turning once, until crisp and golden.
Cool before eating.
why_it_works: Yam's starchier, denser texture gives a genuinely different chip experience from the karle chips in this batch
Baked, not fried, keeping this meaningfully lighter than a traditional suran chip
Uses an underused tuber in a fun, snackable format

name: ZITLAS Roasted Sabudana Papad Snack
description: Sabudana papad roasted directly over a flame instead of deep-fried — a genuinely lighter version of a common Maharashtrian accompaniment, eaten here as a standalone snack.
instructions: Brush the dried sabudana papad lightly with oil.
Roast directly over a low gas flame, turning constantly, until it puffs up and crisps, about 30-40 seconds per papad.
Eat immediately while crisp.
why_it_works: Roasting instead of deep-frying is a genuinely lighter technique for a snack that's traditionally fried

name: ZITLAS Solapur Shenga Chutney Bowl
description: Solapur's famous dry peanut-garlic chutney, served as a standalone bowl with raw onion — a distinct dry, powder-style chutney eaten directly rather than as a spread or dip.

name: ZITLAS Baked Kadboli Rings
description: Spiced rice-and-besan dough shaped into small rings and baked — Maharashtra's traditional festive kadboli snack, made lighter, distinct from the spiral bhakarwadi already in the database by its ring shape and different dough.

Cool completely before storing.

name: ZITLAS Curd Karvand Chutney Dip Snack

name: ZITLAS Sindhudurg Fish Thali Special

name: ZITLAS Kharvas-Inspired Steamed Milk Custard Bowl
description: A ZITLAS adaptation of the traditional Konkan kharvas (made from cow colostrum) using regular milk and egg instead — a genuinely different, more accessible version of a hard-to-source seasonal delicacy.

Steam in a pressure cooker (without the whistle) for 15-18 minutes until set like a custard.

name: ZITLAS Anarsa-Inspired Baked Rice Bites

name: ZITLAS Kaju Modak Bites

name: ZITLAS Jambhul Frozen Sorbet Bowl

name: ZITLAS Chikoo Curd Bowl
